evidence.field: PDF p.76; printed p.64; 八部 entry and continuation checked on PDF p.77
evidence.text: The entry labels 八 a 指事字 and transmits the Shuowen interpretation that its strokes turn away from each other. It explains the graph as separating two strokes to express distinction, then says oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions also borrowed it as a numeral, citing “八羊” and a bronze date. The continuation check found no 八 text continuing on p.77; the 八 entry ends on p.76. This is the book's account, not independent proof that separation preceded numeral use.
evidence.title: 字源, Volume 3 (bibliographic record; 李學勤主編, 天津古籍出版社, 2012, ISBN 9787552800692)

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, 漢字「八」：字形演變
evidence.field: Character evolution account and script categories
evidence.text: The record lists oracle-bone, bronze, Chu manuscript and small-seal forms. Its account interprets 八 as a shape dividing an object into two parts, representing 分, and later borrowed for the numeral. This is the catalog's proposed analysis; the separately inspected CUHK entry reports competing explanations.
evidence.title: 漢字「八」：字形演變

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: Formation analyses and early attestations, lines 171–180
evidence.text: The entry reports the Shuowen account of strokes turning apart, concrete gesture hypotheses, proposals that 八 was an early graph for 分, and a separate proposal connecting its initial sense with 別. It notes that the abstract separation interpretation does not itself identify a concrete pictorial referent. It cites oracle-bone numeral and month uses, including 八犬、八羊 (合集 371正) and 八月 (合集 6), as well as later bronze and Warring States numeral uses. The entry supplies corpus identifiers and context labels, not absolute dates for each object; these attested numeral uses do not establish that separation came first.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 八

evidence.source: Baxter and Sagart, Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1
evidence.field: 八 and 別 entries; Old Chinese and Middle Chinese columns
evidence.text: The author-supplied table lists numeral 八 as Old Chinese *pˤret, Middle Chinese pet, gloss “eight”; 別 ‘separate (transitive)’ as *pret, MC pjet; and 別 ‘be separated (intransitive)’ as *N-pret, MC bjet. Within this specific reconstruction system, the transitive 別 and 八 differ in the pharyngealization marked on the initial, so these entries do not support treating the words as identical in reconstructed pronunciation. This comparison does not decide the historical graph origin or borrowing direction.
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (20 September 2014)

evidence.field: Unihan data organization and readings property documentation
evidence.text: The Unicode specification identifies Unihan as a database of Han-character properties, and explains that its readings category is supplied through versioned Unihan data files. Local tracked HSK extract row U+516B kMandarin bā was checked. The per-character GetUnihanData URL could not be opened in this invocation, so this record documents the official data format, not an independently inspected character-specific web record.

字源 states 八 has historical sound categories 幫組、物部 and 幫組、黠韻, 博拔切; these traditional categories are not merged with Baxter–Sagart notation. Its analysis reads the graph as separation and reports numeral borrowing, while early cited numeral attestations mean that chronology is not independently settled.
No independently verified absolute date for the cited oracle-bone objects, or earlier written 八 use for separation, was obtained. The separation-to-numeral semantic sequence remains a proposal.

External sources differ in analysis: 字源 and Sinica favor a separation/division account, while CUHK preserves competing readings and explicitly questions a settled pictorial origin. This disagreement concerns analysis, not a directly observed depiction of a particular object.
